newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU/Swiss road transit debate remains tricky.
newsitem.headline: EU/Swiss road transit debate remains tricky.

text.p: EU transport ministers' efforts to sort out the problems of trans-Alpine freight traffic remained blocked on Thursday as countries most affected by Switzerland's heavy-lorry ban disagreed on what to do about it.

Ministers heard a report by European Transport Commissioner Neil Kinnock suggesting ways to overcome the conflicting demands of Switzerland, which has held to its 28-tonne limit on lorries, and neighbours Austria and France, who are angry about the resulting diversion of traffic onto their trans-Alpine routes.
Switzerland and the EU's 15 countries have spent months discussing closer ties in a range of areas such as research, trade in processed farm products and free movement of people.

Most areas have been resolved but problems remain in liberalising road transport. The EU wants immediate access to Swiss roads for its 40-tonne lorries while Berne wants the set up of a differentiated charging system penalising dirtier trucks in return for giving up its 28-tonne maximum-weight limit.

A Commission spokesman told reporters that Swiss demands were now intimately linked with the EU's own efforts to set up a tax system favouring cleaner trucks, with low axle weights, over dirtier trucks carrying the higher axle loads which cause greatest damage to roads and bridges.

He said Kinnock had suggested the EU demand of Berne free access for its 40-tonners on Swiss roads from the year 2005 subject to a negotiated maximum charge-per-kilometre which would also apply to French and Austrian Alpine routes to Italy.
In the interim and starting from 1998, some EU 40-tonne lorries would also get access to Swiss industrial centres.

Switzerland, in return for access to EU road freight markets and a guarantee clause in the deal, would develop its promised, combined road/rail transit capacity to offer lorries an alternative route across the Alps, Kinnock said.

In parallel, the EU would raise its current "Eurovignette" lorry charge -- covering Belgium, Denmark, Luxembourg, the Netherlands, Germany and Sweden -- in line with inflation rates since 1993 and would weight the fee to favour cleaner trucks and two, three and six-axled vehicles over four and five-axled ones.

A Eurovignette revision might also help to end Austria's row with the Commission over its Brenner pass lorry tolls, some of which exceed $200 per trip depending on travel time and truck type, which Vienna says reflect the environmental damage caused by trucks but which the Commission deems illegally high.

"Germany, France, Britain, Portugal and Austria were in favour of a proposal that the Brenner pass be classified as an environmentally sensitive route qualifying for a special tariff," the spokesman said, adding: "Does that mean we will accept their tolls? I do not know."
Ministers' talks were due to resume later on Thursday.
